metadata.title: Django - Marking Session as 'modified' + django-silk inspection
metadata.description:

In this video, we'll look at the 'modified' property of session objects, which can be used to tel Django that complex data in sessions (such as lists, nested dictionaries, etc) have been modified. We'll look at using django-silk to inspect the SQL sent to the database on certain session operations.

segments.text: In this video, we're going to look a
little bit more at when Django saves
session information to the database, and
this is going to be the last video in
this small set of videos on Django
sessions. And we're going to look at a
pro tip in this video, and that's the
modified flag that you can add to
Django's session object. And you can use
this when you have complex session
state, such as lists and dictionaries,
and you want to mark that some nested
data has changed, and then flush that
change to the database. So, we're going
to see examples in this video. Before we
get started, if you're finding this
content useful, check out our coffee
page. We've got a link just below the
video. Thank you very much to everybody
who's contributed to that. It's greatly
appreciated. And let's get started
looking at sessions. So, we have this
secret page that we saw in the previous
video, and we're going to work on this
page throughout the video, but for now,
let's go to the Django documentation on
when sessions are saved. Now, by
default, Django only saves to the
session database when the session object
has been modified. That is, if any
dictionary values have been assigned or
deleted. So, for example, here you can
see the session being modified when we
set a key of foo to the value of bar.
So, request.session, if you remember, is
a dictionary-like object called a
session store, and here we can delete a
key from the dictionary. Again, that's
marking the session as being modified,
and Django will then flush that new
change to the database and remove, in
this case, the foo key. So, whenever you
assign to a key, such as this here, even
if you're assigning an empty dictionary
in this case, you're noting that the
session has been modified, and Django
will flush that change to the database.
But here is the small gotcha. If you
have nested data, for example, in the
foo dictionary that we set up above
here, if you then add a key to that
nested dictionary called bar, and then
set it to a value, in this case, the
session is not modified. So, if your
session state contains nested
dictionaries like this, you need to tell
Django when you're changing the nested
data, and you can do it by setting this
modified flag to true. So, you can see
request.session.modified,
we're setting it to true here, and that
will then tell Django we need to save
the session data to the session back-end
in the database. Now, we're going to
look at a small demo that's going to use
Django Silk to inspect the requests and
the SQL. But before we move on to that,
notice this setting. It's called session
save every request, and if you want to
save the session data on every request,
you can set this to true. By default,
this is set to false. That would give
you a safe way to update the session,
but it comes with a downside of sending
some session updates SQL to the database
on every single request, which is maybe
not something you really need to do
here. Now, let's look at a very small
example with Django, and we're going to
go to that secret view that we have in
the application that is protected by
login required. And let's just start by
setting a session variable here. So,
request.session, and let's say the user
has set their theme preference on the
front-end, and we're going to set that
to dark. So, essentially, we're changing
it to dark mode here. This is a canned
example, I'm not going to deny it, but
let's see what happens when we go to
this secret page. So, let's refresh this
page, and what what I have loaded here
is Django Silk, which we can use to
inspect the requests that have been sent
to the application. So, if we refresh
this summary page, we've now got one
request that was sent, and we can then
go to that and inspect some of the
details and profiling that's involved in
this request. And one of the options
here is to look at the SQL. Now, notice
this update statement here. This is
updating the Django session database
table that we saw in the initial session
video. That's because we are using the
database as our session engine. So, when
we modify data like this on a per
visitor basis, that's ultimately going
to be stored in that table. Now, if we
go back to the application and again
refresh this page, I'm going to go back
to the Django Silk summary page, and
we're going to see again that an update
is sent to the session table. And the
reason for that is because it appears
that we are amending the theme key of
request.session, even though we're
setting it to the same value. So, every
time we change a key in the in the
session object, it's going to send that
update to the database. And for code
like this, it's going to be a wasted
query to the database. What we can do
instead is we can check if theme is
already in the request.session
dictionary. Now, the way to do that is
to use an if statement. So, we can check
if theme is in request.session,
and we can tab this over, but we don't
need to change this because we're going
to set the theme option if it's not in
the request.session. So, instead of if
it's in request.session, we're going to
check if it's not yet been set. So, if
the theme is not in request.session, we
will set it for the first time. And now,
if we go back to this page and refresh
the page, we can go back to Django Silk,
and if we look at the summary page here,
this has only two queries, and we are no
longer issuing the update statement. And
by the way, if you want to know more
about Django Silk, I'll leave a link to
the video we did on this topic in the
comments. So, this is more performant if
you're just hardcoding something like
this, because you no longer need to send
that update statement to the database on
every single request to this view. Now,
with objects like lists and nested
dictionaries of data in the session,
this update that we saw before is not
automatic. So, I'm going to change this
up slightly. We're going to look at a
key called items, and if that's not in
request.session, we're going to set that
key in request.session to an empty
Python list. Now, if we save that and go
back to the secret page here, let's
refresh the page, and then if we go back
to Django Silk, we can look at the most
recent request, and notice again we now
have an update to the Django session
table. But that's not going to happen if
we go back and refresh one more time. If
we go back to the requests page and
refresh here, we no longer get that
update because it's already written the
items to the session, and this if
statement prevents it from being written
again. So, the items key in the session
is now an empty list. What happens if we
try and append an item to that? So, I'm
going to look at request.session, and
let's extract the items key here, and
then because that is a list in Python,
we can call the dot append method. And
let's append an item here called item
one. Now, request.session is a
dictionary-like object. What I'm going
to do after we append that item is I'm
going to print out the dictionary.items
method. So, what that returns is the
keys and values in the dictionary. Let's
print that to the terminal. And now,
we're going to go back to the secret
page, and we're going to see what
happens. So, let's refresh this page,
and I know I'm refreshing this page
randomly. Nothing's happening on the
page itself, but if we go back to the
most recent request, which is this one
here, and look at the SQL, we don't get
any updates to the session table. We can
see a select to the session table, but
that happens on every request. But there
are no updates to the table, even though
we have appended an item to the items
key in request.session. Now, if we open
the terminal, we're going to see the
dictionary items that were printed on
line 35 here. So, let's have a look at
these, and notice here, if we look at
the items key in the session, it does
appear that the list contains an item
here called item one. So, that's kind of
weird because we're not updating the
database, but we have appended this item
to the session in memory. But we're
going to see the problem if we go back
to the secret page and refresh again.
So, when we refresh this page, again
this view is going to be called, and
what's going to happen is we're going to
try and append item one again to
request.session at the items key. And if
we go back to the terminal, we can see
again, this was the initial print
statement. In the second print
statement, again item one is the only
item in that key. Now, what we would
expect to see is item one added on the
initial request, and then on the second
request, we expect to see the list
containing two elements, both with the
string item one. But that's not what's
happening because when these items are
appended, Django is not saving that to
the database. And the reason it's not
saving is because Django does not detect
that appending to a list, for example,
is something that should trigger a flush
of the session data. But what we can do,
as we saw in the documentation, is we
can take request.session, and in the
view, we can set modified to true. Now,
when we do that, if we go back to the
page here, I'm going to refresh this
page, and then let's go back to Django
Silk, and let's go back to the request
summary and go to the most recent
request. And when we look at the SQL,
notice the update statement has been
sent to the database, and we have now
updated the session table for the user
who has that key. Now, if we go back to
the terminal, let's go and expand this
and go to the bottom. So, I had to find
that there. Basically, what's happening
is that we have the item one now in the
items key, but if we go back to this
page here and refresh the page, and then
look at the terminal again, we see what
we expected to see initially, and that's
that the items list is now stateful.
It's being saved to the database, which
means when the second append comes in,
Django is able to pull out the initial
state, and then append to that state.
So, we now have the proper behavior
here. Each time the user goes to this
page, it's appending these items to the
list, and all we need to do is when
we're modifying that state, such as
adding and removing elements from a list
or a nested dictionary, we just set the
modified flag to true, and Django will
then save the session data to the
database, and that allows you to
preserve those updates. So, that's a
short demo, but it's useful knowledge
for Django, although maybe not the most
exciting topic in the world. One thing I
want to say is that something like an
LLM might be able to give you this code,
but would you understand it? And just to
share my opinion at the end here, I
think with the job market as it is,
understanding these concepts can really
set you apart and can help you get
success in this industry in what is
becoming more and more competitive and a
more AI-dominated industry. So, this has
been a small video with some useful
Django knowledge. If you have any other
requests, let me know in the comments
for Django material. And if you want to
